title: When Operators Build Their Own FMS, the Incumbent Stack Has Already Lost the Argument
summary: FlyExclusive's in-house Contrails FMS is more than an efficiency story — it's evidence that the flight ops software market still isn't delivering what fast-moving operators actually need at the cockpit level.
body_markdown:
The most pointed signal that a vendor market isn't working isn't a bad review or a lost contract. It's when your customers stop waiting and start building.

That's essentially what FlyExclusive has done. The Raleigh-based private jet operator — running 72 aircraft at roughly 200 legs per day — has built a proprietary flight management system called Contrails FMS to handle scheduling, optimization, and pilot-facing workflow. Aviation Week reported this week that the company is now deepening that investment with AI, with the goal of having the system handle flight-plan loading and aircraft readiness before passengers even board. At the pace FlyExclusive operates, saving ten minutes per leg across 200 daily departures isn't a marginal efficiency gain — it compounds into something that moves the business.

## The build-vs-buy signal is worth taking seriously

The instinct in aviation technology commentary is to treat operator-built software as a curiosity — a boutique solution that works at small scale but couldn't possibly threaten the established platforms. I'd push back on that read. When an operator at FlyExclusive's operational tempo decides the right answer is to build its own FMS rather than buy from the market, that's not primarily a story about engineering ambition. It's a statement about fit. Something in the available stack — whether the integration model, the update cadence, the data architecture, or the underlying assumptions about how a fast-cycle fractional and charter operation actually flows — wasn't close enough.

This isn't isolated. Having spent years delivering and deploying flight ops software across different operator types, I've seen firsthand how the gap between a platform's design assumptions and an operator's actual workflow tends to widen exactly where the operation is moving fastest. The vendors who built their platforms for scheduled commercial aviation — where turnaround times are long, fleet types are predictable, and ops cycles run in hours — often struggle to adapt their architecture for operators whose entire value proposition is speed and flexibility.

## The AI layer changes the calculus

What makes the FlyExclusive story particularly worth watching isn't the FMS itself — it's what happens when a purpose-built system starts absorbing AI. Contrails FMS already handles the scheduling and optimization layer. Adding AI to pre-load flight plans and coordinate pilot readiness before passenger boarding is a meaningful step toward what I'd call proactive cockpit state — the idea that the aircraft and its software are actively ready before the crew needs to act, rather than waiting on crew input to trigger the next step.

That's a genuinely different philosophy from how most EFB and flight-planning platforms are designed. The dominant model is still reactive: the pilot opens the app, pulls the plan, reviews it, accepts it. Proactive cockpit state inverts that — the system knows the departure window, monitors the variables, and surfaces a ready state. It requires tight integration between scheduling, flight planning, and pilot-facing tools that commercial EFB vendors have mostly gestured at rather than delivered.

FlyExclusive's Contrails FMS is trying to close that loop in-house because buying a closed integration from separate vendors would require more coordination than the company has patience for. That's an honest admission about where the market stands.

## What this means for the vendor side

The risk for the established flight-ops software market isn't that FlyExclusive's system becomes a competitor — it almost certainly won't, at least not in the near term. The risk is the pattern it represents. As AI tooling gets cheaper and more accessible, the barrier to building purpose-fit flight ops software continues to fall. An operator with strong engineering talent and a clear operational problem can now get further, faster, than they could five years ago. The incumbents' historical advantage — years of aviation-specific data and regulatory depth — still matters enormously for safety-critical functions. But for the workflow and optimization layers that sit above the safety floor, that moat is narrowing.

The vendors who respond to this by doubling down on API openness and genuine configurability will hold operators in. The ones who treat integration as a negotiated add-on will keep losing customers to their own build teams.
